blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
• Sampling error is the difference between a sample statistic and the population parameter that arises by chance, because only part of the population was measured. For one sample it is x̄ − μ, a number you never know, since μ is unknown.
  • The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of the sampling error over all possible samples of the same design: the typical size of the sampling error (defined formally in §6.7). You cannot know the sampling error of your sample, but you can estimate its typical size.
  • Non-sampling error is every error not caused by sampling: an incomplete or outdated frame (coverage error), non-response, measurement and interviewer error, and data-entry or processing error (Banda, 2003). It occurs in a census too.
  • Bias, in the design sense used in this section, is a systematic error from how units were selected (selection bias) or measured (measurement bias) that pushes results in one direction. It is the systematic part of non-sampling error, and it does not shrink as the sample grows.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Sampling error is the honest static of measuring a part instead of the whole (recall §1.3: a statistic differs from its parameter). It is random in direction, and it shrinks as the sample grows. Bias is different in kind: it is baked into how the sample was chosen or measured, it points in one direction, and a bigger sample of the same flawed kind only gives a more precisely wrong answer. The total error of a survey is sampling error plus non-sampling error, and “if not properly controlled nonsampling error can be more damaging than sampling error for large-scale household surveys” (Banda, 2003).

A second meaning of “bias” appears in §6.5 and Chapter 7: estimator bias, the gap between the average of an estimator over repeated samples and the parameter. The divide-by-n variance is biased in this sense (recall §3.6.2), but its bias shrinks to zero as n grows. When this book says bias “does not shrink with n”, it means design bias; say which sense you mean.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
A genuinely random sample of 50 children’s weights has a mean that differs a little from the true mean, by chance. That is sampling error, and 500 children instead of 50 shrinks it roughly threefold (§6.7 shows why: √10 ≈ 3.2). If the “random” sample was drawn only from a well-funded urban clinic, missing poorer rural children who tend to weigh less, the mean will be too high whatever the sample size. That is selection bias.

Sampling error Standard error Non-sampling error
What it is x̄ − μ for this sample SD of x̄ − μ over repeated samples Frame, non-response, measurement, processing errors
Known for your sample? No Estimated (s/√n for a mean) Rarely; assessed by re-survey or checks
Direction Random Not applicable (a spread) Often systematic (bias)
Larger n Shrinks on average Shrinks as 1/√n Does not shrink; may grow

points.html: A larger sample reduces sampling error and does nothing to fix design bias. Sample size and design quality are separate levers; one cannot make up for the other. A convenience sample of 10,000 can be less trustworthy than a random sample of 100.

Non-sampling error “may increase with increases in sample size” (Banda, 2003): more interviewers and more forms mean more chances to err. This is the reason a well-run sample can beat a census (§6.1).
Probability sampling controls selection bias; adequate sample size controls sampling error; training, piloting, supervision and re-checks control non-sampling error.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 6.3

questions.prompt: State the single structural difference between quota sampling and stratified sampling, and explain the specific bias that snowball sampling risks.
questions.answer: Both fix numbers per subgroup; stratified sampling selects randomly within each subgroup, quota sampling fills each quota by convenience. Snowball sampling is biased towards well-connected members of the hidden population: people who are socially isolated, or whose networks do not overlap with the initial contacts, are rarely reached however many referral chains are followed.

questions.prompt: The true mean weight of under-five children in a district is 11.8 kg. A team weighs 2,000 children attending a well-funded urban clinic and gets a mean of 12.6 kg; its standard error is 0.04 kg. How large is the error of this estimate, how much of it could sampling error plausibly explain, and would weighing 8,000 clinic children fix it?
questions.answer: Total error = 12.6 − 11.8 = 0.8 kg. The SE is the typical size of the sampling error (§6.4): about 0.04 kg. 0.8 kg is 0.8 ÷ 0.04 = 20 times that typical size, so chance explains almost none of it: it is selection bias (the clinic’s children are better-off and heavier). With 8,000 clinic children the SE falls to 0.04 ÷ √4 = 0.02 kg (four times the sample halves the SE), but the bias of about 0.8 kg remains. The answer becomes more precisely wrong. Only a better design (a probability sample of the district’s children) fixes it.

questions.prompt: Name three sources of non-sampling error in a household survey and say which of them would also affect a census.
questions.answer: Any three of: coverage (frame) error, such as households missing from an outdated list; non-response (absent or refusing households); measurement error (a faulty scale, a leading question, interviewer effects, recall error); processing error (data entry, coding). All of them can affect a census too; only sampling error is absent from a census.
